name: Akye
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Only Blench 2018 (noun affixes) cited anywhere; rogerblench.info is now a domain-squat casino site; no phonology of Ake located

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. Ake page, rogerblench.info (Internet Archive copy 2025-05-23)
sources.note: Index page only: lists the unpublished 'Ake wordlist' and material-culture photographs; no other Ake documents exist on Blench's site (the Internet Archive's index listing of the Ake folder saved).

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.1 languoid page akee1238 and hh.bib records (w:Blench:Ake, wsoc:Decker:Akye)
sources.note: Bibliographic only: Glottolog lists no grammar, phonology or sketch for Akye (Glottolog lists no grammar, sketch or phonology); the two language-specific items are the Blench wordlist and the Decker et al. survey.
Nothing; cites only Ethnologue and Blench 2018.

sources.citation: Decker, Ken, Innocent Jonah, John Muniru, Yakubu Danladi, Benard Abraham, David Onoja & Christina Riepe. 2021. A Sociolinguistic Profile of the Akye (Ake) [aik] Language of Nasarawa State, Nigeria. Journal of Language Survey Reports 2021-042. 51 pp.
sources.note: Only other language-specific publication; contains a wordlist appendix and a 'Linguistic relationships' section that may carry transcription notes on tone (a stress statement is unlikely but this is the only unread candidate). PDF is open in a browser but blocked by an automated-access block JS challenge by automated download; a human download would close the gap.
sources.venue: Journal of Language Survey Reports 2021-042. 51 pp

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2018. Nominal affixes and number marking in the Plateau languages of Central Nigeria. In John R. Watters (ed.), East Benue-Congo: Nouns, pronouns, and verbs, 107-172. Berlin: Language Science Press. doi:10.5281/zenodo.1314325
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Section 2.8.3 Eggonic (pp. 157-159) treats Ake fossil noun prefixes only; mentions that former V- prefixes 'often have two distinct tones'.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2006/2007. The Ake language of Central Nigeria and its affinities. Draft circulated for comment, printout 5 September 2007. Cambridge: Mallam Dendo. 27 pp. (Glottolog refs 18452 / 18453)
sources.note: Nothing. Section 3 Phonology (p. 3) gives vowels, consonants and 3.3 Tones: 'Ake has three level tones, and glide tones that arise from sequences of level tones.' The words stress/accent/prosody do not occur anywhere in the text; the author warns the phonology is 'tentative' and that tones are generally unmarked in the wordlist.
sources.venue: Draft circulated for comment, printout 5 September

sources.citation: Sommer, Gabriele. 1992. A Survey on Language Death in Africa. In Brenzinger (ed.), Language Death, 301-413. Mouton de Gruyter. doi:10.1515/9783110870602.301
sources.note: Not opened (paywalled overview of endangerment); a language-death survey, not a description.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2019 (ed. IV). An Atlas of Nigerian Languages. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation (Glottolog ref 672361 lists the 2011 ed. III)

sources.note: Would only confirm the Ake entry's classification and sources; no phonology expected. The rogerblench.info host is now a domain-squat, so an archived copy would be needed.
